passages.title: The return of the evening class
passages.text:
[A] Twenty years ago, the community college in the fictional town of Ashford offered more than eighty evening courses, from car maintenance to conversational Italian. By 2015, that number had fallen to fewer than thirty. Online tutorials had made it easy to learn almost anything at home, and many adults said they were simply too busy to spend two hours in a classroom after work.

[B] Since then, however, enrolment has risen every year. The college now runs fifty-five evening courses, and some, such as pottery and first aid, have waiting lists. The director, Maria Lund, believes the main reason is social. “People can learn facts online,” she says, “but they cannot easily make friends there. Many of our students live alone or have moved to the area recently. The class is where they meet people.”

[C] Price also plays a part. Most courses cost between forty and ninety pounds for ten weeks, and students over sixty pay half price. The college keeps fees low by using volunteer assistants and by sharing rooms with the local secondary school, which are empty in the evenings. Courses that lead to a qualification, such as accounting, are more expensive because examinations must be paid for.

[D] Not all subjects have recovered. Language courses, once the college’s most popular area, still attract fewer students than before, probably because free translation apps and language programmes are widely available. On the other hand, practical subjects that need equipment or close supervision – woodwork, cookery and photography – are more popular than ever.

[E] The college has also changed when and how it teaches. Some courses now start at half past six rather than seven, so that parents can be home earlier, and several combine online video lessons with a practical session every two weeks. According to the college’s own survey, students on these mixed courses were just as satisfied as those attending every week in person.

[F] Lund admits that the growth may not continue. The college’s funding from the regional government is reviewed every three years, and the next decision is due soon. For now, though, she is optimistic. “Every September,” she says, “I see people who arrived as strangers leave the building together, still talking about what they made.”

[G] Other colleges in the region are watching Ashford closely. Two have already copied its idea of starting earlier in the evening, and one has begun inviting former students back as volunteer assistants. Whether the same approach will work in larger cities, where people have many more choices of things to do after work, remains an open question.

passages.title: Museums you are allowed to touch
passages.text:
[A] For most of their history, museums asked visitors to look but not touch. Objects were placed behind glass, guards watched the rooms, and signs reminded children to keep their hands to themselves. In the last thirty years, a different kind of museum has spread around the world: the hands-on science centre, where pressing buttons, building structures and testing ideas is the whole point of a visit.

[B] Supporters say these centres reach people who would never enter a traditional museum. Visitor surveys at one large centre in the fictional city of Port Hallam found that forty per cent of adult visitors had not been to any museum in the previous five years. Families also stay longer: the average visit lasts three hours, compared with about seventy minutes at the city’s art gallery.

[C] The educational value of all this activity is harder to judge. A team of researchers watched children in one gallery and recorded what they did at each exhibit. Many children ran from one button to the next, spending less than thirty seconds at each display, and few read the explanations. When the researchers interviewed them afterwards, most could describe what had happened at an exhibit but not why it had happened.

[D] Small changes made a big difference. When staff members or volunteers were present to ask simple questions – “What do you think will happen if you make the ramp steeper?” – children stayed at exhibits up to four times longer and were much more likely to explain the science correctly. Exhibits that asked visitors to make a prediction before acting had a similar effect, even without an adult present.

[E] Traditional museums have taken note. Several now offer handling sessions in which visitors may hold real fossils or historical tools under supervision, and some have added touch-screen displays beside their glass cases. Directors stress that the aim is not to turn every museum into a playground, but to give visitors a reason to think about what they are seeing.

[F] Science centres are also changing the way they measure success. Rather than counting only tickets sold, some now record how long visitors spend at each exhibit and invite a sample of families to answer a few questions as they leave. These measures are less simple than visitor numbers, but they show whether people have actually understood something new, which is the reason most centres were built in the first place.
